task: Fewest multiplications for polynomial multiplication over GF(p), by searching for a spanning set of lower total rank
source: Produced by `reproduce/measure.py`, which runs `minimise-rank fixtures/<name>.tensor` once per fixture, sequentially, and records the provenance block below.
why: Nothing in the repository could re-derive the published numbers. These are computed from the committed fixtures by code the CI runs, and each result is checked to still generate the map it came from.
machine: Single core of a 12th Gen Intel i5-12450H at 2.2 GHz, which is the machine Table 1 was measured on.
warning: Times are cumulative: step 3 includes steps 1 and 2.
retired_by_the_bounds: Seven published counts were retired or corrected on 2026-08-19, and this says what happened to each. `reproduce/measure.py --check` re-derives `exact_search` and `famous_tensors` now as well as `fixtures`; it did not before, which is how thirty-odd counts in these two blocks went unchecked and these seven went stale unnoticed. **Four are refutations `rank_lower_bound` now refuses before the search opens a node**, so the count is 0 with no search time beside it, and that is a better published figure than the one it replaces: a floor returned in milliseconds is a stronger statement than a tree walked to the end for a minute. They are `f2_5x5` at 9, 10 and 11 (was 1, 959 and 459 239 nodes, at 0.0003 s, 0.17 s and 77.4 s), GF(16) at 7 (was 1 897 576 nodes, 34.5 s), cyclic 5 at 7 (was 461 251 nodes, 51.4 s) and `<2,2,3>` at 8 (was 446 923 nodes, 53.1 s). **Three are `decided` node counts that fell because the search reaches the same answer sooner**: `f2_2x3` 3 to 2, `gf4_multiplication` 3 to 2, `gf8_multiplication` 1606 to 329, with every verdict and product count unchanged and `f2_2x2` still at 1. What still reproduces exactly: `<2,2,2>` at 25 399 nodes to rule out 6 and 7 436 to find 7, and every heuristic step count here except `<2,3,3>`'s, which nothing asks. **Dated, because two of these are today's and five are older.** `f2_5x5` at 10 and 11 were live measurements until the Griesmer floor moved that map from 10 to 12 on 2026-08-19 (`rank_metric_bound/`): a build of the tree as it stood the night before still walks 459 239 nodes to refuse 11. The other five were already stale before that session began, and the same build proves it, refusing GF(16) at 7, cyclic 5 at 7 and `<2,2,3>` at 8 from the bounds and giving 2, 2 and 329 nodes on the three `decided` maps. The counts here were refreshed by `measure.py --counts`, which rewrites counts and leaves timings alone, so the microsecond figures beside the three corrected `decided` counts are older than the counts and were not re-measured: this machine had three other agents on it, and MEASURING.md does not accept a timing taken there. `counts_provenance` names the commit that produced the counts and says as much.
steps: Step 1, greedy smallest basis: walk the span from lowest rank upwards, keeping whatever is not already spanned.
Step 2, minimise over the rank-one maps already inside the map.
Step 3, minimise over every rank-one map of the shape.
readings: Step 3 improved the answer in two of the four cases, by one product each time: 16 to 15 on f2_3x8 and 11 to 10 on f3_3x6. On f2_5x5 and f2_4x7 it confirmed what step 2 already had.
Step 3 is where almost all the cost is. It costs between 58 and 184 times what steps 1 and 2 cost together, so any effort spent making it faster is spent on the part that mostly does not pay.

What the orbit quotient is worth, and where. Refuting 6 products on <2,2,2> costs 25 399 nodes plainly and 648 under `-s matmul 2 2 2`, 39.2x fewer for the identical verdict. Finding 7 costs 7 436 and 3 167, only 2.3x. The quotient pays on the proof far more than on the witness, which is the shape you would expect: a refutation has to walk every branch, and every branch that is another branch in a different basis is walked again, while a search that stops at the first decomposition stops before most of that repetition. Both rows are re-derived by `reproduce/measure.py --check`, and the verdict is checked on both sides rather than recorded: a quotient that changed the answer would be a bug, not a speed-up.
limits: Every step is greedy and nothing here proves a result is optimal. The bilinear rank problem is open, and none of this settles it.

methods.heuristic: Greedy, three steps, no optimality guarantee, except step 1, which is a matroid greedy and therefore gives a minimum-weight basis of span(T).
methods.exact: Complete decision: is there an algorithm with exactly k products? An implementation of a pre-existing published algorithm. Exponential, so it decides small maps outright and bounds large ones.

exact_search.note: Produced by `decide-rank`, searching from the map itself rather than from any heuristic answer, so these are statements about the maps.

decided.why_trustworthy: Karatsuba's answer, and 2n-1 = 3 is a lower bound, so 3 is optimal.
A 2x3 product: five products instead of six.
The bilinear complexity of GF(4) over GF(2) is classically 3.
The bilinear complexity of GF(8) over GF(2) is classically 6.

bounded.conclusion: No algorithm with 9, 10 or 11 products exists, each refused by `rank_lower_bound` before the search opens a node, and none with 12 exists either, that one by exhaustion. So the rank is at least 13. Nine and ten were exhaustions and eleven was a 77 second one until 2026-08-19; see `retired_by_the_bounds`. The heuristic exhibits only 14, and `lower-the-bound` exhibits 13 in 80 nodes, so this repository proves rank = 13 on both sides. Table 1 of Barbulescu, Detrey, Estibals and Zimmermann (2012) gives 27 decompositions at 13 and agrees.
bounded.not_decided: whether 13 products suffice. Exhibiting one is what would close this map here, and it has not been run. Ruling out 12 has: 146402553 nodes, NO and exhaustive, on 2026-08-19. A refutation's node count does not depend on the thread count, measured in `exhaustive_search/what-threads-change.md`, so that figure is the tree's; the run itself took 535.59 s on six cores with `--node-limit 300000000`, which is not the one-core figure MEASURING.md publishes and is recorded here as what it is. This file previously priced ruling out 12 at about seven hours and recorded it as never run, and before that recorded it as done at 146402553 nodes and 3610.2 s when no such run had happened. The node count in that retracted figure was right and only the seconds were invented; the seven hours came from the general leaf's 5900 nodes a second, where the GF(2) leaf walks the same question at 459239 nodes in 7.69 s and repriced it at about 40 minutes on one core.

pipeline.note: The rank search emits the encoding operators; the sparsification is what they are for.

famous_tensors.note: The tensors the complexity literature argues about, run through both searches over GF(2). A bilinear map is an order-3 tensor, so they need a constructor and nothing else: make-tensor --matmul n m k and --cyclic n. Prose: famous_tensors/.

runs.reading: Strassen's 7 and Winograd's proof that 6 is impossible, both reproduced from nothing in 0.55 s. No single rank-one map strictly improves the tensor, so the step 3 shortlist is 0 of 225 and the descent cannot take a first step. Two things cross the plateau it is stuck on, and their costs are published rather than quoted: flip_graph/results.json.
Rank >= 9 here. Ruling out 9 is about 1.4e8 nodes, some 4.6 hours, and was not run.

exact.why: its span has dimension 6, so target 10 is C(32193, 4) = 4.5e16 leaves. The depth is the gap between the span and the target, and four levels over a pool this size is not a long run, it is never.

heuristic.step_3: stopped at 45 minutes; projected 4.2 hours from the measured 2x3x3 scan, and one independent test per candidate, so it parallelises

runs.known: open: 19 <= rank <= 23, and >= 20 over F2 since 2026
runs.reading: Out of reach exactly: ruling out 10 is 2.6e5 nodes against a pool of 261121, about 10 hours.
Decided exactly. The border rank of 2 is invisible to this search, which is why it is worth listing.

9 <= rank <= 10. `rank_lower_bound` returns the 9 in milliseconds, where refusing 7 was 461 251 nodes and a minute; see `retired_by_the_bounds`. The heuristic works here, unlike on matrix multiplication.

exact.rule_out_8: 105 600 301 nodes, and the wall clock beside them, are published once, in `satisfiability/results.json`, which is the row `reproduce/measure.py` re-derives and where the `--node-limit 200000000` behind the count is recorded. This file used to restate the pair and stated the seconds as 2325.7 against that file's 2328 for the one run, which is what publishing a number twice costs. It is a pointer now rather than a copy.

runs.known: >= 8 by de Groote, since 2n-1 is attained only for n <= q/2 + 1
runs.reading: Decided exactly: 9. The exact search ruled out everything below, 5, 6 and 7 free from the polynomial bounds and 8 by exhaustion; the heuristic supplied the 9, and neither method could have done it alone.

refused.tensor: <4,4,4>, where AlphaTensor found 47 products over Z2
refused.bytes: 8.2 TiB, as the tool reports when refusing
refused.reading: Refused by the memory budget rather than attempted. This is the allocation that had no guard.

famous_tensors.finding: The heuristic and the exact search fail on different tensors. On every matrix multiplication tensor whose pool scan can finish the heuristic does not improve the naive count at all, with an empty shortlist out of 225, 945 and 32193 candidates, and the tool says why: not one of the 225 rank-one maps improves <2,2,2>, so a first-improvement greedy has nowhere to step. Step 1 is a matroid greedy and therefore optimal over bases of span(T), which is exactly the ceiling: 8 is the true minimum over those bases, and Strassen's 7 products are not a basis of span(T) but a rank-one basis of a 7-dimensional space containing it. The exact search finds that in 0.14 s.

provenance.protocol: one core, fastest of three, quiet machine. See MEASURING.md.

counts_provenance.covers: The counts in this file and the invocations that produced them, and nothing else. Every `seconds` field here is older than this block and was not touched: a count is exact arithmetic and comes out the same on any machine, a timing does not, so `--counts` refreshes the first and leaves the second exactly as measured. What produced the timings is the `provenance` block.
counts_provenance.protocol: counts only: exact arithmetic, one run each, the machine irrelevant.
